Let $M$ be a boundaryless $n$-manifold, $R$ a commutative unital ring, and $K\subseteq M$ compact. Then $H_i(M,M\setminus K;R)=0$ for $i>n$, and restriction from $H_n(M,M\setminus K;R)$ to all local stalks at points of $K$ is injective. Every continuous section $s$ of the local $R$-homology system on $M$ is realized by a unique class $s_K$ in this relative group.

In particular an $R$-orientation determines a unique $[M]_K$ restricting to its generator at each point of $K$. These classes commute with restriction for compact-set inclusions and split over the finitely many components meeting $K$. No AC is needed.

A continuous map of pairs $f:(X,A)\to(Y,B)$, meaning $f(A)\subseteq B$,
induces $f_*:H_n(X,A;G)\to H_n(Y,B;G)$ for every $n$. Identity maps and
composites induce identity maps and composites.

The **relative singular homology group** of $(X,A)$ in degree $n$ is
$$H_n(X,A;G):=H_n(C_\bullet(X,A;G))=\ker\bar\partial_n/\operatorname{im}\bar\partial_{n+1}.$$
Equivalently, a relative cycle is an ordinary finite chain $c$ with
$\partial c\in C_{n-1}(A;G)$, modulo adding a chain in $A$ and an ordinary
boundary.

If $Z\subseteq X$ and $\overline Z\subseteq\operatorname{int}_X(A)$, then
inclusion $(X-Z,A-Z)\to(X,A)$ induces isomorphisms
$H_n(X-Z,A-Z;G)\cong H_n(X,A;G)$ for every $n$.

Let $M$ be an $n$-manifold with boundary and $x\in M$. For any commutative unital coefficient ring $R$,
$$H_k(M,M\setminus\{x\};R)\cong\begin{cases}R,&x\in\operatorname{int}M\text{ and }k=n,\\0,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
The boundary subset is independent of charts, and a nonempty manifold's dimension is intrinsic. Homeomorphisms preserve boundary and, for nonempty manifolds, dimension. A manifold is boundaryless exactly when it is locally Euclidean of its specified dimension. Dimension is not intrinsic for the empty space, and the zero coefficient ring cannot detect boundary or dimension; use integral coefficients for these conclusions. No AC is assumed.

derivations.claim: If $f^{-1}(y)\cap U=\varnothing$, then $K=\varnothing$ and $H_d(U,U\setminus K)=H_d(U,U)=0$, so $D(f,U,y)=0$. For the identity and $y\in U$, $K=\{y\}$ and the induced map sends the chosen local orientation generator to itself, so $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$.

Under the additivity hypotheses, $K$ is the disjoint union of $K_i=K\cap U_i$. The closed set $Z=U\setminus(U_1\cup U_2)$ has closure in $U$ disjoint from $K$: the compact set $K$ lies in the open set $U_1\cup U_2$. Excision [F3] identifies $H_d(U,U\setminus K)$ with $H_d(U_1\cup U_2,(U_1\cup U_2)\setminus K)$. Since $U_1,U_2$ are disjoint open sets, every singular simplex in their union lies in exactly one of them, so this relative group and its chains split as the direct sum of the two relative groups. The unique orientation class [F1] therefore corresponds to $[U_1]_{K_1}+[U_2]_{K_2}$. The restrictions of $f$ commute with the inclusions of these pairs, so functoriality [F2] maps this sum to the sum of the two target classes. Their integer coefficients consequently satisfy $D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y)$.

For moving-target invariance set $g_t(x)=H_t(x)-y(t)$; translation identifies the target generator with the standard generator at $0$. The zero set $S=\{(t,x):g_t(x)=0\}$ is a closed subset of compact $[0,1]\times\overline U$ and is disjoint from $[0,1]\times\partial U$. Thus its projection $K_*\subset U$ is compact. Every $g_t$ defines a map of the fixed pair $(U,U\setminus K_*)$ into $(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\})$. The singular prism operator for the homotopy satisfies $\partial P+P\partial=(g_1)_\#-(g_0)_\#$; each prism over a simplex in $U\setminus K_*$ avoids $0$, so the chain homotopy descends to relative chains. Hence $(g_0)_*=(g_1)_*$ on $H_d(U,U\setminus K_*)$. Restriction compatibility in [F1] sends $[U]_{K_*}$ to $[U]_{K_t}$ for the actual time-$t$ zero set, so these two induced integers are exactly $D(H_0,U,y(0))$ and $D(H_1,U,y(1))$. They are equal, proving moving-target invariance.

The target group is $\mathbb Z$ by [F4]; the source class is unique by [F1]; and the induced map exists by [F2]. Thus the integer in the Statement is well-defined. Steps 1.1–3.1 establish all asserted properties.

derivations.claim: Suppose first that $M>0$ and $w$ has not reached zero by $t_0+2M/\eta$. Integrating $w'\ge\eta/2$ gives $w(t_0+2M/\eta)\ge w(t_0)+M\ge0$, contradicting the assumed strict negativity before the first crossing. Hence the first crossing time $\tau$ exists and satisfies the stated bound. If $M=0$, then $w(t_0)=0$ and $\tau=t_0$.

On $[t_0,\tau]$, $w$ is strictly increasing with $w'\ge\eta/2$, so it is an admissible absolutely continuous time change. Its inverse satisfies $dt/dw\le2/\eta$. If $L>0$, set $p=\epsilon+Lq$. The inequality for $q$ gives $dp/dw\le(2L/\eta)|w|p$, and integration from $w(t_0)$ to $0$ yields $p(\tau)\le\epsilon e^{LM^2/\eta}$. Rearranging gives $q(\tau)\le\epsilon(e^{LM^2/\eta}-1)/L$. If $L=0$, direct integration gives $q(\tau)\le(2\epsilon/\eta)\int_{w(t_0)}^0|s|ds=\epsilon w(t_0)^2/\eta\le\epsilon M^2/\eta$. The same bounds hold with zero right-hand side when $M=0$.

derivations.claim: If $y=f(x)$ for $x\in\operatorname{spt}\mu$ and $V$ is any open neighborhood of $y$, continuity makes $f^{-1}(V)$ an open neighborhood of $x$. Hence $f_\#\mu(V)=\mu(f^{-1}(V))>0$, so $y\in\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$. Taking the closure relative to $Y$, since support is closed, $\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}\subseteq\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$.

The complement of $\operatorname{spt}\mu$ has $\mu$-measure zero: every point in it lies in a zero-measure open neighborhood, and the countable relative Euclidean basis gives a countable cover by zero-measure basis sets. If $y\notin\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}$, choose an open neighborhood $V$ disjoint from that closure. Then $f^{-1}(V)\subseteq X\setminus\operatorname{spt}\mu$, so $f_\#\mu(V)=0$ and $y\notin\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)$. Thus $\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)\subseteq\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and define
$$\nu_f(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu \qquad (A\in\mathcal A).$$
Then $\nu_f$ is a measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A)$ be a measurable space. A **signed measure** on
$(X,\mathcal A)$ is a function
$$\nu:\mathcal A\longrightarrow \overline{\mathbb R}$$
such that:

1. $\nu(\varnothing)=0$;
2. $\nu$ takes at most one infinite sign: either $\nu(E)\neq-\infty$ for every
   $E\in\mathcal A$, or $\nu(E)\neq+\infty$ for every $E\in\mathcal A$;
3. for every pairwise disjoint sequence $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ in
   $\mathcal A$,
   the series on the right is defined in the extended reals and
   $$\nu\left(\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \nu(E_n)$$
   ([[def-extended-reals]]).

The second and third clauses are load-bearing, not stylistic: together they
rule out the undefined form $(+\infty)+(-\infty)$ and require the disjoint
series to exist before countable additivity is asserted.

The next proposition proves the extra fact that if
$\nu(\bigcup_n E_n)$ is finite, then the real series $\sum_n \nu(E_n)$
converges absolutely in the sense of
[[def-absolute-and-conditional-convergence]].

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

The class $L^1(\mu)$ is a complex vector space, and the Lebesgue integral is
complex-linear on it:
$$\int (\alpha f+\beta g)\,d\mu=\alpha\int f\,d\mu+\beta\int g\,d\mu \qquad(\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb C,\ f,g\in L^1(\mu)).$$

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

derivations.claim: The coordinate $w$ is measurable, so $w_+$ and $w_-$ are nonnegative measurable functions. By [F1], $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ are measures, and [F2] gives $\alpha_\mu(\Theta),\beta_\mu(\Theta)\le\int|w|d\mu<\infty$.

For each measurable $B$, $w=w_+-w_-$ and both integrals are finite, so $\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w d\mu=\alpha_\mu(B)-\beta_\mu(B)$. Countable additivity of both finite measures makes their difference countably additive with finite real values, hence a finite signed measure by [F3]. For every $B\in\mathcal T$ and every countable measurable partition $(B_j)$ of $B$, $\sum_j|h^1(\mu)(B_j)|\le\sum_j(\alpha_\mu(B_j)+\beta_\mu(B_j))=\alpha_\mu(B)+\beta_\mu(B)$; taking the supremum in [F4] proves the stated pointwise total-variation bound. The weighted penalty inequality follows by monotonicity of the nonnegative integral, first for simple nonnegative weights and then by increasing simple approximation. For a finite-valued simple $\varphi$, linearity [F5] and the definitions of $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ give $\int\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int w\varphi d\mu$. For general bounded measurable $\varphi$, choose $M$ with $|\varphi|\le M$ and partition $[-M,M]$ into finitely many intervals of length at most $1/n$; assigning one endpoint on each measurable inverse image gives a finite-valued simple $\varphi_n$ with $\|\varphi_n-\varphi\|_\infty\le1/n$. The errors in the two $\alpha_\mu,\beta_\mu$ integrals are at most $(\alpha_\mu(\Theta)+\beta_\mu(\Theta))/n$, and the error in the $w\varphi$ integral is at most $\int|w|d\mu/n$. Letting $n\to\infty$ proves the identity.

Let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and strongly measurable. Simple approximants to $\varphi$ and to the measurable scalar coordinate $w$ show that $w\varphi(\theta)$ is strongly measurable; moreover $\|w\varphi(\theta)\|\le|w|\|\varphi\|_\infty$, so [F6] makes it Bochner integrable. For each $z\in\mathcal H$, [F7] moves the bounded functional $x\mapsto\langle z,x\rangle$ inside that Bochner integral, and step 2.1 identifies the resulting scalar integral with the pairing in the Definition. Equality of all inner products proves the displayed feature-moment factorization.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and with differential bounded on every sublevel set of $R$: for each $c\ge0$,
$$\sup\{\|dR_z\|_{\mathcal H^*}:z\in\mathcal H,\ R(z)\le c\}<\infty.$$ In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: First, $\Phi$ is Borel measurable with values in the separable space $\mathcal H$. Fix a countable dense sequence $(h_j)$ in $\mathcal H$; the map assigning to $\Phi(u)$ a nearest point among $h_1,\ldots,h_k$, breaking ties by least index, is finite-valued and measurable, and its error tends to zero as $k\to\infty$. Thus $\Phi$ is strongly measurable. Moreover, $\|\Phi(w,\theta)\|\le\|\varphi\|_\infty|w|$. A probability law with finite second moment has $\int|w|d\mu\le(\int|w|^2d\mu)^{1/2}<\infty$ by Cauchy–Schwarz. Thus [F3] gives existence of its feature moment, while $0\le V\le\|\widetilde V\|_\infty|w|$ gives a finite penalty; $R$ is finite-valued. This proves the asserted well-definedness for every law in the Statement. By [A1] and [F1] choose couplings $\pi_n$ of $\mu_n$ and $\mu$ with $\delta_n^2=\int(|w-w'|^2+|\theta-\theta'|^2)d\pi_n\to0$. By [F2], the coupling marginal identities hold also for these Bochner feature integrals: apply a bounded linear functional, use the scalar marginal identity, and identify the vectors by all such evaluations. Consequently [F4] and the pointwise bound $$\|w\varphi(\theta)-w'\varphi(\theta')\|\le\|\varphi\|_\infty|w-w'|+\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)|w'|\,|\theta-\theta'|$$ give $$\|m_{\mu_n}-m_\mu\|\le\left(\|\varphi\|_\infty+\operatorname{Lip}(\varphi)\Bigl(\int|w'|^2d\mu(w',\theta')\Bigr)^{1/2}\right)\delta_n\longrightarrow0.$$ The second-moment factor belongs to the fixed limit marginal and is finite, with no bound on the diameter or interior of $\Theta$ required.

Since $\bigl||w|-|w'|\bigr|\le|w-w'|$, the same estimate with scalar $\widetilde V$ in place of $\varphi$ gives $\int Vd\mu_n\to\int Vd\mu$. Step 1.1 gives convergence of feature moments in $\mathcal H$; continuity of $R$ therefore gives convergence of the risk terms. Adding the two limits proves $F(\mu_n)\to F(\mu)$. Under the full feature-energy hypotheses, the identical feature and penalty integrals are finite by step 1.1, so the finite branch in that definition gives exactly this $F$. If $\Theta=\varnothing$, no law in the Statement exists and the assertion is vacuous; zero maps, zero weights and singleton or lower-dimensional $\Theta$ are included in the estimates.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Then there exist positive
measures $
u^+,
u^-:(X,\mathcal A)	o[0,+\infty]$, at least one finite on $X$, such that
$$
u=
u^+-
u^-,$$
and $
u^+\perp 
u^-$.

These measures are unique: if $
u=\mu-\eta$ with positive measures
$\mu\perp\eta$, then $\mu=
u^+$ and $\eta=
u^-$.

The following conditional assertion is choice-free: if a Hahn partition
$X=P\sqcup N$ is supplied, the formulas $
u^+(E)=
u(E\cap P)$ and
$
u^-(E)=-
u(E\cap N)$ construct these unique measures. Comparing
two supplied mutually singular positive decompositions also requires no AC.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable space and let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative measure on $(\mathbb R\times\Theta,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal T)$ such that $\int|w|d\mu(w,\theta)<\infty$. Set $w_+=\max(w,0)$ and $w_-=\max(-w,0)$, and define finite nonnegative measures on $\Theta$ by

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

The partially one-homogeneous signed projection is

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

$\int_\Theta\varphi\,dh^1(\mu):=\int_\Theta\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int_\Theta\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int_{\mathbb R\times\Theta}w\varphi(\theta)d\mu(w,\theta).$

Put $\lambda_\mu=\alpha_\mu+\beta_\mu$, so $\lambda_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}|w|d\mu$. Its total variation satisfies $|h^1(\mu)|(B)\le\lambda_\mu(B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal T$. Therefore $\int\widetilde Vd|h^1(\mu)|\le\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$ for every bounded nonnegative measurable $\widetilde V$.

If $\mathcal H$ is a separable real Hilbert space and $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ is bounded and strongly measurable, then for every $z\in\mathcal H$ the feature moment satisfies $\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu)$, with the scalar integral defined above. The raw measures $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ record positive and negative parameter weights before cancellation and need not be mutually singular; for example, if $\mu$ assigns mass one to each of $(1,\theta_0)$ and $(-1,\theta_0)$ and zero elsewhere, then $\alpha_\mu=\beta_\mu$ both assign mass one to $\theta_0$ while $h^1(\mu)=0$. Thus the signed projection does not by itself determine a penalty of the form $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$.

Let $X,Y$ be Banach spaces, let $T:X\to Y$ be bounded and linear, and let $f$
be Bochner integrable. Then $T\circ f$ is Bochner integrable and, for every
measurable $E$,

$$T\left(\int_Ef\,d\mu\right)=\int_E Tf\,d\mu.$$

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. Because
$|\nu|$ is a measure ([[thm-total-variation-is-a-measure]]), define
$$L^1(\nu):=L^1(|\nu|)$$
using the published meaning of $L^1$ from [[def-l-one-of-a-measure]].

If $f\in L^1(\nu)$, choose complex simple functions $s_n$ as in
[[thm-l-one-functions-admit-dominated-complex-simple-approximations]] with
$\int |f-s_n|\,d|\nu|\to0$. The simple-integral bound
[[prop-simple-integrals-are-bounded-by-total-variation]] makes
$(\int s_n\,d\nu)$ a Cauchy sequence in $\mathbb C$, and its limit is
independent of the chosen approximating sequence. Define
$$\int f\,d\nu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int s_n\,d\nu.$$

For a measurable set $E\in\mathcal A$, define
$$\int_E f\,d\nu:=\int f\mathbf 1_E\,d\nu.$$

Let $\nu$ be a signed measure or a complex measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$. For
$E\in\mathcal A$, define its **total variation on $E$** by
$$|\nu|(E):=\sup\left\{\sum_{n=0}^\infty |\nu(E_n)|:\ (E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\text{ is a countable measurable partition of }E\right\},$$
where, for a signed measure, the term $|\nu(E_n)|$ means the ordinary absolute
value when $\nu(E_n)\in\mathbb R$ and means $+\infty$ when
$\nu(E_n)\in\{+\infty,-\infty\}$; for a complex measure it is the usual complex
modulus. A countable measurable partition of $E$ means:

1. each $E_n$ lies in $\mathcal A$;
2. the sets $E_n$ are pairwise disjoint;
3. $E=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n$.

The sum on the right is a nonnegative extended series, so it is always defined
in $[0,+\infty] \subseteq \overline{\mathbb R}$.

For signed measures, a later proposition shows that finite partitions already
suffice. For complex measures, that finite-partition shortcut is not built into
the definition here.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. Let $f,g:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable and let $c\ge0$.

1. If $f\le g$, then $\int f\,d\mu\le\int g\,d\mu$.
2. If $c>0$, then $\int cf\,d\mu=c\int f\,d\mu$. For $c=0$,
   the integral of the zero function is $0$. Neither clause forms the
   undefined extended-real product $0\cdot(+\infty)$.

Let $
u$ be a signed measure on $(X,\mathcal A)$, with Jordan decomposition
$
u=
u^+-
u^-$. Then for every measurable $E$:

1. $$|
u|(E)=
u^+(E)+
u^-(E);$$
2. the same value is the supremum over finite measurable partitions of $E$;
3. $$
u^+(E)=\sup\{
u(F):F\subseteq E,\ F\in\mathcal A\};$$
4. $$
u^-(E)=-\inf\{
u(F):F\subseteq E,\ F\in\mathcal A\}.$$

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.

Define $\rho(u)=u/|u|$ for $u\ne0$. The **two-homogeneous projection** of $\mu$ is the set function on Borel $A\subseteq\mathbb S^{d-1}$

$$h^2(\mu)(A)=\int_{\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}}\mathbf1_A(\rho(u))|u|^2d\mu(u).$$

It is a finite nonnegative Borel measure: the integrand defines the weighted measure $|u|^2\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, and preimages under the continuous map $\rho$ preserve disjoint unions; its total mass is at most $\int|u|^2d\mu$. Mass at $u=0$ contributes zero. If $\Phi$ or $V$ is positively two-homogeneous, this projection records its radial integral on the sphere; the exact identities are stated separately.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable space and let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative measure on $(\mathbb R\times\Theta,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal T)$ such that $\int|w|d\mu(w,\theta)<\infty$. Set $w_+=\max(w,0)$ and $w_-=\max(-w,0)$, and define finite nonnegative measures on $\Theta$ by

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

The partially one-homogeneous signed projection is

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

$\int_\Theta\varphi\,dh^1(\mu):=\int_\Theta\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int_\Theta\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int_{\mathbb R\times\Theta}w\varphi(\theta)d\mu(w,\theta).$

Put $\lambda_\mu=\alpha_\mu+\beta_\mu$, so $\lambda_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}|w|d\mu$. Its total variation satisfies $|h^1(\mu)|(B)\le\lambda_\mu(B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal T$. Therefore $\int\widetilde Vd|h^1(\mu)|\le\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$ for every bounded nonnegative measurable $\widetilde V$.

If $\mathcal H$ is a separable real Hilbert space and $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ is bounded and strongly measurable, then for every $z\in\mathcal H$ the feature moment satisfies $\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu)$, with the scalar integral defined above. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: On $\mathbb R^d\setminus\{0\}$, write $u=|u|\rho(u)$. Positive two-homogeneity gives $\Phi(u)=|u|^2\Phi(\rho(u))$ and $V(u)=|u|^2V(\rho(u))$; at $u=0$ both vanish. Integrating these identities and applying the definition of $h^2$ proves both displayed projection identities.

For weak convergence on the compact sphere, the masses $h^2(\mu_n)(\mathbb S^{d-1})$ are bounded. The continuous map $\Phi|_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ has compact image in $\mathcal H$. Given $\epsilon>0$, choose finitely many vectors $g_j=\Phi(\theta_j)$ whose open $\epsilon$-balls cover that image and put $U_j=\{\theta:\|\Phi(\theta)-g_j\|<\epsilon\}$. Define $r_j(\theta)=\operatorname{dist}(\theta,\mathbb S^{d-1}\setminus U_j)$ when the complement is nonempty, and $r_j\equiv1$ when $U_j=\mathbb S^{d-1}$. The continuous functions $\psi_j=r_j/(\sum_i r_i)$ are well-defined because the finite open sets cover the sphere, and $\psi_j(\theta)>0$ only when $\theta\in U_j$. Therefore $\|\Phi(\theta)-\sum_j\psi_j(\theta)g_j\|<\epsilon$ uniformly. Weak convergence gives convergence of each scalar coefficient $\int\psi_jdh^2(\mu_n)$, hence strong convergence of the approximating vector integrals. The uniform approximation error is at most $\epsilon$ times the uniformly bounded masses, so $\int\Phi dh^2(\mu_n)\to\int\Phi d\nu$ in norm. Since $V|_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}$ is continuous, weak convergence also gives $\int Vdh^2(\mu_n)\to\int Vd\nu$. Continuity of $R$ proves the energy limit.

In the partially one-homogeneous case, fix $z\in\mathcal H$ and apply [F2] to the bounded scalar function $\psi(\theta)=\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle$. This gives the displayed feature identity for every $z$, hence equality of the Hilbert-valued feature moments because inner products determine vectors. For the penalty, $|w|-w=2w_-\ge0$, and [F2] applied to $\widetilde V$ gives $\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu-\int\widetilde Vdh^1(\mu)=2\int w_-\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu\ge0.$ If $h^1(\mu_n)$ converges against bounded continuous scalar tests, testing against $\langle z,\varphi(\cdot)\rangle$ for each $z\in\mathcal H$ proves weak convergence of the feature moments. Under the additional AC, closed-Euclidean, separable-Hilbert assumptions in the Statement, [F4] improves this to norm convergence. Let $\mu_1$ assign mass one to $(1,\theta)$ and let $\mu_2$ assign mass two to $(1,\theta)$ and mass one to $(-1,\theta)$. Then both have $h^1$ equal to the measure assigning mass one to $\theta$, while their $|w|$ penalties for $\widetilde V\equiv1$ are $1$ and $3$, respectively. Thus $h^1$ convergence alone cannot imply penalty or energy convergence.

Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. The source Assumptions 2.1 use the stronger maximal bound for the ambient potential subgradients before adding the domain indicator; that original bound implies the bounded-selection condition used here. Taking a supremum over the relative-domain supporting set would instead include unbounded normal vectors at proper-domain boundaries and would incorrectly exclude the constrained branch. All original source hypotheses and conclusions are retained by this sufficient, weaker growth convention. For a Borel set $A\subseteq\Omega$, write $\mathcal P_2(A)$ for the Borel probability measures on $\mathbb R^d$ concentrated on $A$ and having finite second moment.
For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Write $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ for curves whose restriction to every finite interval $[0,T]$ belongs to $AC^2([0,T];\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d))$ in the $W_2$ metric. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite energy, define $F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u)$ on $\Omega$, and extend this potential by $+\infty$ off $\Omega$. Its constrained subdifferential at $u$ is the local Fréchet subdifferential of $F'(\mu)+\iota_\Omega$ defined in the feature-measure-energy convention. A Wasserstein gradient flow from $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ is a curve $t\mapsto\mu_t$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}([0,\infty);(\mathcal P_2(\mathbb R^d),W_2))$, with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$, for which there is a Borel velocity $v_t(u)$ satisfying the finite-action continuity equation and $v_t(u)$ equals the negative minimum-norm element of $\partial(F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega)(u)$ for $dt\,d\mu_t(u)$-almost every $(t,u)$. This definition does not assert that the energy is displacement convex.

Assume DC. Let $X$ be a Banach space, $Y$ a normed space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of bounded linear operators $X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). If $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|Tx\|<\infty$ for every $x\in X$, then $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|T\|<\infty$, where the norm is [[def-operator-norm]].

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: The natural partial-model cutoffs $Q_r=[-r,r]\times\Theta$ satisfy the feature-energy conditions: their distance enlargement is $Q_{r+r'}$, boundedness of $\varphi,\widetilde V$ bounds $\Phi,V$ there, and the bounded Lipschitz first derivatives give Lipschitz $d\Phi$ on each slab. The ambient potential has a local supporting vector $(\operatorname{sign}(w)\widetilde V,|w|\nabla\widetilde V)$ off $w=0$, and $(0,0)$ at $w=0$; its norm is bounded by $C(1+r)$. These vectors belong to the relative supporting set by global semiconvexity, so no bound on normal vectors is needed. Thus bounded initial weights supply the common-cutoff hypothesis of [F1]. The path $t\mapsto m_{\mu_t}$ is continuous on $[0,T]$, so its differential image $\{dR_{m_{\mu_t}}:0\le t\le T\}$ is compact and bounded. Boundedness of $\varphi,\widetilde V$ and [F4] give a finite $B_T$ with $|\dot w|\le B_T$ for every characteristic. Choose $\alpha>r_0+B_TT$. Characteristics from $K_0$ have $|w_t|<\alpha$ for $0\le t\le T$, while characteristics starting on either plane $w=\pm\beta$ remain outside the slab $|w|\le\alpha$ for every $\beta>\alpha+B_TT$.

In the bounded branch, $K_0$ is compact because it is closed and contained in the compact set $[-r_0,r_0]\times\Theta$. Thus $X_t(K_0)$ is compact and closed, so [F1]–[F2] give $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=X_t(K_0)$. The Neumann premise makes the angular characteristic tangent to $\partial\Theta$. In local boundary charts the characteristic equation restricted to $\mathbb R\times\partial\Theta$ therefore has a solution starting at every boundary point; ambient uniqueness identifies it with the characteristic from that point. This proves the forward invariance of the boundary used below.

In the unbounded branch use $\psi(	heta)=	anh|	heta|\,	heta/|	heta|$ for $	heta
e0$ and $\psi(0)=0$. This maps $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ diffeomorphically onto the open unit ball. Its radial and tangential differential eigenvalues are $\operatorname{sech}^2|	heta|$ and $	anh|	heta|/|	heta|$, both tending to zero at infinity. A bounded $C^1$ function with Lipschitz derivative has bounded derivative: Taylor's inequality in the unit direction of its derivative would otherwise force its bounded range to grow without bound. Apply this to scalar evaluations of $\varphi$ and to $\widetilde V$; hence the angular gradients $
abla G_f$ are bounded on bounded sets of $f$. For each $f$, the assumed $C^1$ limit of $G_f(r\cdot)$ gives pointwise convergence of bounded linear operators $f\mapsto\langle f,\varphi(r\cdot)angle$ into $C^1(\mathbb S^{d-2})$. On bounded radial intervals their operator norms are bounded by local $C^1$ regularity; convergence at infinity makes the family pointwise bounded. By [F5] the operator norms are uniformly bounded, and the convergence is uniform on the compact set $\{dR_{m_{\mu_t}}:0\le t\le T\}$ by finite-net approximation. The partial characteristic equations for $w>0$ and $w<0$ are $\dot w=-G_{a_t,+}(	heta)$, $\dot	heta=-w
abla G_{a_t,+}(	heta)$ and $\dot w=G_{a_t,-}(	heta)$, $\dot	heta=-|w|
abla G_{a_t,-}(	heta)$, respectively, where $G_{a_t,+}=a_t[\varphi]+\widetilde V$ and $G_{a_t,-}=-a_t[\varphi]+\widetilde V$. At $w=0$, the scalar inclusion is $\dot w\in-\partial_w(a_t[\varphi(	heta)]w+\widetilde V(	heta)|w|)$ and $\dot	heta=0$; the pointwise minimum-norm choice is used by the flow definition, but the vector-field selection can jump across $w=0$. The compactified angular speed is $D\psi(	heta)\dot	heta$, which tends uniformly to zero as $|	heta|	o\infty$ for bounded $w$. The coefficients of the limiting scalar inclusion converge uniformly on the compact set of risk gradients. Monotonicity of the subdifferential of the convex function $w\mapsto aw+V|w|$ gives $|w_1(t)-w_2(t)|\le |w_1(0)-w_2(0)|+\int_0^t(|a_1-a_2|+|V_1-V_2|)ds$ for two solutions, so the scalar characteristics converge continuously to their unique boundary limit. Write $Y_t$ for the characteristic flow in $(w,\psi(	heta))$ coordinates; it extends continuously to the closed unit ball, with lateral angular coordinate fixed at the boundary.

In the unbounded branch the original map $X_t$ is closed on $\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^{d-1}$. If $X_t(w_n,\theta_n)$ converges to a finite point, [F4] bounds $w_n$; compactness of the closed unit ball gives a convergent subsequence of $\psi(\theta_n)$. Its limit cannot lie on the boundary because $Y_t$ preserves that boundary, while the image limit is finite. Hence a subsequence of $(w_n,\theta_n)$ converges in the original domain; closedness follows. Now [F1]–[F2] give $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=X_t(K_0)$ in this branch as well.

Fix any $\beta>\alpha+B_TT$. In either branch, use $Y_s=X_s$ in the bounded case and the compactified characteristic $Y_s$ from step 3.1 in the unbounded case. Put $\widehat K_0^{\beta}=K_0$ in the bounded case and let $\widehat K_0^{\beta}$ be the closure of $(\mathrm{id}\times\psi)(K_0)$ in $[-\beta,\beta]\times\overline D$ in the unbounded case. This is closed; any added limit points lie on the lateral boundary because $K_0$ is closed in the original domain. Work in $U_\beta=(-\beta,\beta)\times D$, where $D=\operatorname{int}\Theta$ in the bounded case and $D$ is the open unit ball in the compactified case. Let $A_\beta$ be the component of $U_\beta\setminus\widehat K_0^{\beta}$ containing the connected positive face $\{\alpha\}\times D$. The positive face lies in $A_\beta$ because it misses $\widehat K_0^{\beta}$. No point of the negative face lies in $A_\beta$: a path in $A_\beta$ from $-\alpha$ to $+\alpha$ would have a subpath between its last crossing of $w=-r_0$ and its first later crossing of $w=r_0$, wholly inside the original box and disjoint from $K_0$, contrary to the assumed separation. Here components of an open subset of Euclidean space are path connected, since each path component is open and its complement is a union of open path components. The boundary satisfies $\partial A_\beta\subseteq\widehat K_0^{\beta}\cup\partial U_\beta$. At time $s\in[0,T]$, the image of the original part of $\widehat K_0^{\beta}$ lies in $|w|<\alpha$, the horizontal boundary planes $w=\pm\beta$ map outside $|w|\le\alpha$, and the lateral boundary maps into itself by steps 2.1–3.1. The added compactification points are on that lateral boundary. Therefore every target on either $\alpha$ face avoids $Y_s(\partial A_\beta)$. The definition and properties of $D$ in [F3] give $D(Y_t,A_\beta,y)=1$ on the positive face and $D(Y_t,A_\beta,y)=0$ on the negative face.

Suppose a path in $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ joins the negative to the positive $\alpha$ face without meeting $X_t(K_0)$. In the bounded branch, compactness and positive distance from the closed support let us perturb the path by an arbitrarily small convex interpolation toward a fixed interior point of $\Theta$; the perturbed path stays disjoint from the support and has endpoints in $D$. In the unbounded branch its compact image already lies in the open ball after applying $\psi$. Stop the path at its first visit to the positive face, and let $m$ be its minimum $w$-coordinate. Choose $\beta>\max\{\alpha,-m\}+B_TT$ and use the construction of step 5.1 with this $\beta$. The target path is contained in $U_\beta$ and avoids the images of the horizontal boundary planes. In the unbounded case it lies in the open ball, so it also avoids the added lateral limit points of $Y_t(\widehat K_0^{\beta})$; its remaining points avoid that image by the assumption that the original path misses $X_t(K_0)$. Degree invariance along this target path would make its endpoint values of $D(Y_t,A_\beta,\cdot)$ equal, contradicting the values $0$ and $1$ from step 5.1. Thus every such path intersects $X_t(K_0)=\operatorname{spt}\mu_t$.

Assume AC and the full feature-measure energy hypotheses. Let $\mu_0\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ have finite energy and be concentrated on $Q_{r_0}$. There is a unique global curve $\mu:[0,\infty)	o\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ in $AC^2_{\mathrm{loc}}$ with $\mu_{t=0}=\mu_0$ that solves the continuity equation with the negative minimum-norm subgradient velocity of the extended potential $F'(\mu_t)+\iota_\Omega$. For every finite $T$, the curve is concentrated on some $Q_{r(T)}$ and satisfies
$$F(\mu_t)-F(\mu_s)=-\int_s^t\int|v_q(u)|^2d\mu_q(u)dq\qquad(0\le s\le t\le T).$$
For any $\mu_0,
u_0$ concentrated on the same $Q_{r_0}$, their flows obey $\sup_{0\le t\le T}W_2(\mu_t,
u_t)\le e^{K_TT}W_2(\mu_0,
u_0)$ for a finite constant $K_T$ depending only on $T$, $r_0$, and a common upper bound for the initial energies. Consequently, W2-convergent initial laws in a common $Q_{r_0}$ have flows converging uniformly in W2 on every compact time interval.

Assume AC and the feature-measure energy hypotheses. Fix $r>0$ and a nonempty closed convex constraint $D\subseteq\Omega$. For every continuous moment path $m:[0,T]	o\mathcal H$, the nonautonomous inclusion
$$\dot X(t)\in-\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(X(t))-d\Phi_{X(t)}^*
abla R(m(t))$$
has a unique forward solution from each $X(0)\in D\cap Q_r$; its characteristic map is jointly continuous in $(t,X(0))$ and locally Lipschitz in the initial point on each $Q_r$. Let $\mu_t$ and $
u_t$ be two finite-action solutions on $[0,T]$ of the continuity equation with laws concentrated on $D\cap Q_r$ and velocities
$$v_t^\alpha(x)=-\operatorname{argmin}\{|q|:q\in d\Phi_x^*
abla R(m_{\alpha_t})+\partial_{\lambda_V}(V+\iota_D)(x)\},\qquad\alpha\in\{\mu,
u\},$$
where $m_\alpha=\int\Phi\,d\alpha$. The full shifted minimum selection is Borel; it need not be continuous in position. Each finite-action PDE solution with a continuous prescribed feature moment is the pushforward by its unique characteristic map. For starts in $D\cap Q_r$, these characteristics remain in a larger $Q_R$ uniformly on compact time intervals, and their velocity is the negative full shifted minimum almost everywhere. The same construction applies directly to any continuous forcing $a(t)\in\mathcal H$ in place of $
abla R(m(t))$. Then for all $t\in[0,T]$,
$$W_2(\mu_t,
u_t)\le e^{(C_r-\lambda_V)t}W_2(\mu_0,
u_0),\qquad C_r=L_rA_r^2+N_rB_r.$$
Here $A_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|d\Phi\|$, $B_r=\operatorname{Lip}_{Q_r}(d\Phi)$, $M_r=\sup_{Q_r}\|\partial V\|$ in the bounded-selection convention, and $L_r,N_r$ are respectively a Lipschitz constant and a norm bound for $dR$ on the closed convex hull of $\Phi(Q_r)$. In particular, the localized measure-valued flow is unique for each initial law. The estimate does not assume that $v_t$ is continuous in position.

Assume AC. Let $T>0$ and let $(\mu_t,v_t)$ be a narrowly continuous finite-action solution of the continuity equation on $[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d$. There is a Borel probability law $\eta$ on $C([0,T];\mathbb R^d)$ such that $(e_t)_\#\eta=\mu_t$ for every $t$, and for $\eta$-almost every path $\gamma$, $\gamma$ is absolutely continuous and $\dot\gamma(t)=v_t(\gamma(t))$ for almost every $t$. Its expected path action equals the Eulerian action:
$$\int\!\int_0^T|\dot\gamma(t)|^2dt\,d\eta(\gamma)=\int_0^T\!\int|v_t(x)|^2d\mu_t(x)dt.$$

Let $X\subseteq\mathbb R^k$ and $Y\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be closed Euclidean subspaces. Let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative Borel measure on $X$, define $\operatorname{spt}\mu=\{x:\mu(U)>0\text{ for every relatively open neighborhood }U\text{ of }x\}$, and let $f:X\to Y$ be continuous. Define the pushforward by $f_\#\mu(A)=\mu(f^{-1}(A))$ for Borel $A$. Then

$$\operatorname{spt}(f_\#\mu)=\overline{f(\operatorname{spt}\mu)}.$$

Let $d\ge1$, let $U\subset\mathbb R^d$ be bounded and open, and let $f:\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ be continuous. For $y\notin f(\partial U)$, put $K=f^{-1}(\{y\})\cap U$ and define $D(f,U,y)$ by

$$f_*[U]_K=D(f,U,y)[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}\quad\text{in }H_d(\mathbb R^d,\mathbb R^d\setminus\{y\};\mathbb Z),$$

where $[U]_K$ is the unique relative orientation class restricting to the standard local generator on $K$, and $[\mathbb R^d]_{\{y\}}$ is the positive local generator. This integer is well-defined. It is nonzero only if $f^{-1}(y)\cap U\ne\varnothing$, and $D(\operatorname{id},U,y)=1$ whenever $y\in U$. If $U_1,U_2\subset U$ are disjoint bounded open sets, $y\notin f(\partial U_i)$ for $i=1,2$, and every point of $f^{-1}(y)\cap U$ lies in $U_1\cup U_2$, then

$$D(f,U,y)=D(f,U_1,y)+D(f,U_2,y).$$

If $H:[0,1]\times\overline U\to\mathbb R^d$ and $y:[0,1]\to\mathbb R^d$ are continuous and $y(t)\notin H_t(\partial U)$ for every $t$, then $D(H_0,U,y(0))=D(H_1,U,y(1))$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Since $R(m_{\mu_t})\le F(\mu_0)$, $\|dR_{m_{\mu_t}}\|$ is bounded on $[0,T]$ by [F1]. Differentiating $\Phi(ru)=r^2\Phi(u)$ gives $d\Phi_{ru}=r\,d\Phi_u$. If $\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$, substitute $y=rz$ into its defining inequality and use $V(rz)=r^2V(z)$; division by $r^2$ shows $r\zeta\in\partial_{\lambda_V}V(ru)$, and applying the same argument with $1/r$ proves equality of the scaled subdifferentials. The feature-energy bounds on the unit sphere therefore imply $|v_t(u)|\le C|u|$ uniformly on $[0,T]$. Along a characteristic, $r(t)=|X_t(u_0)|$ obeys $|r'(t)|\le Cr(t)$ whenever $r(t)>0$. Grönwall gives $e^{-Ct}|u_0|\le|X_t(u_0)|\le e^{Ct}|u_0|$; the lower bound prevents a nonzero trajectory from reaching zero, while two-homogeneity fixes the zero trajectory.

By [F3], the flow law has a path-space representation concentrated on AC trajectories solving its velocity equation, with initial law $\mu_0$. Each such path solves the nonautonomous characteristic inclusion for the moment path $m_{\mu_t}$; uniqueness in [F2] makes it $t\mapsto X_t(x)$ from its initial point $x$. Therefore $\mu_t=(X_t)_\#\mu_0$. The compact set $K$ has compact image $X_t(K)$; [F4] gives $\operatorname{spt}\mu_t=\overline{X_t(K)}=X_t(K)$. Continuity on $[0,T]\times K$ makes $M_K=\sup_{s\le T,u\in K}|X_s(u)|$ finite.

Let $C_\infty$ be the unbounded component of $\mathbb R^d\setminus K$. It is unique because the complement of a sufficiently large ball is connected. It is an open connected subset of Euclidean space, hence path connected: small open balls show that each path component is open, and its complement, being a union of the other path components, is open as well. No point of $C_\infty$ lies in $B(0,r_a)$: a path in $C_\infty$ from such a point to a point outside $B(0,r_b)$ would contain a subpath from $r_a\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $r_b\mathbb S^{d-1}$ lying in $C_\infty$ and avoiding $K$, contrary to the initial separation. Choose $\alpha>\max(r_b,M_K)$ and then $\beta>e^{CT}\alpha$. Set $A=B(0,\beta)\cap C_\infty$. Its boundary lies in $K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$, and $A\cap B(0,r_a)=\partial A\cap B(0,r_a)=\varnothing$.

For $y\in\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$, $y\in A$ and $X_s(\partial A)$ avoids $y$ for all $s\le T$: $X_s(K)\subset B(0,M_K)\subset B(0,\alpha)$, while the radial lower bound sends $\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ outside $B(0,\alpha)$. Homotopy invariance [F5] gives $D(X_t,A,y)=D(\operatorname{id},A,y)=1$. Choose $0<\eta<e^{-CT}r_a$. For every $y\in B(0,\eta)$ and $x\in\partial A$, $|X_s(x)|\ge e^{-Cs}|x|\ge e^{-CT}r_a>\eta$, so the target avoids $X_s(\partial A)$. Since $B(0,r_a)\cap A=\varnothing$, the identity degree there is zero; hence $D(X_t,A,y)=0$.

Consider any path from $\eta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ to $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$ and stop it the first time it reaches $\alpha\mathbb S^{d-1}$. Before that time it stays in $\overline{B(0,\alpha)}$, which is disjoint from $X_t(\beta\mathbb S^{d-1})$. If the stopped path avoided $X_t(K)$, then $\partial A\subset K\cup\beta\mathbb S^{d-1}$ would imply that it avoided $X_t(\partial A)$. The degree along that moving target path would be constant by [F5], contradicting its endpoint values $0$ and $1$ from step 4.1. Thus every such path meets $X_t(K)=\operatorname{spt}\mu_t$, proving separation.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $d\ge2$, let $\mathcal H$ be a real Hilbert space, let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, and let $\Phi:\mathbb R^d\to\mathcal H$ and $V:\mathbb R^d\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous and positively two-homogeneous. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\lambda$ on $\mathbb R^d$ with finite second moment, define the feature-measure energy
$$F(\lambda):=R\!\left(\int_{\mathbb R^d}\Phi(u)d\lambda(u)\right)+\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\lambda(u).$$
The integrals are finite because the continuous two-homogeneous maps grow at most quadratically. For every such $\mu$,

$$\int_{\mathbb R^d}\Phi(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\Phi(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta),\qquad\int_{\mathbb R^d}V(u)d\mu(u)=\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}V(\theta)dh^2(\mu)(\theta).$$

If $(\mu_n)$ is a sequence of such measures and $h^2(\mu_n)$ converges weakly as finite measures on the compact sphere to a finite nonnegative measure $\nu$, then the feature integrals converge in Hilbert norm, the regularizer integrals converge, and $F(\mu_n)\to R(\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}\Phi d\nu)+\int_{\mathbb S^{d-1}}Vd\nu$. The continuity of $R$ is the risk premise used for this energy conclusion; it holds in particular under the feature-energy hypotheses.

For the partially one-homogeneous model, let $\Theta$ be a closed Euclidean subset, let $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ be bounded and norm-continuous into a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\widetilde V:\Theta\to[0,\infty)$ be bounded and measurable. Put $\Phi(w,\theta)=w\varphi(\theta)$ and $V(w,\theta)=|w|\widetilde V(\theta)$. For every finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R\times\Theta$ with $\int|w|d\mu<\infty$ and every $z\in\mathcal H$, the exact feature identity is
$$\left\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\right\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu),$$
using the scalar pairing defined in the partial projection, and the penalty inequality is $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu\ge\int\widetilde Vdh^1(\mu)$. Define the lifted energy in this model by $F(\mu)=R(\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu)+\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$. If finite signed projections $h^1(\mu_n)$ converge narrowly to $\nu$, meaning convergence against every bounded continuous real test on $\Theta$, then their feature moments converge weakly in $\mathcal H$ when $\varphi$ is bounded and continuous. If AC holds, then for closed Euclidean $\Theta$ and bounded norm-continuous $\varphi$ into a separable Hilbert space, they converge in Hilbert norm. Signed projection convergence alone does not imply penalty or full energy convergence for arbitrary lifts.

**Assume the Axiom of Choice.** Let $X$ be a nonempty compact metric space, let $Y$ be a metric space, and let $\mathcal F\subseteq C(X,Y)$. The closure of $\mathcal F$ in the uniform topology is compact if and only if $\mathcal F$ is metric-equicontinuous and pointwise relatively compact.

The projected-limit theorem [F2] applies to this weak limit. If it denotes the limit by $
u$, then for every continuous test on the compact sphere both $
u$ and $ho:=h^2(\mu_\infty)$ give the limit of the same integrals $\int fdh^2(\mu_t)$. Testing $f\equiv1$ shows that both have the same total mass $M$. If $M=0$, both finite nonnegative measures are zero. If $M>0$, then $

u=ho$. Viewed as a measure on $\mathbb R^d$, this limit globally minimizes $F$ over all finite nonnegative Borel measures, exactly as asserted by the theorem.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. Let $d\ge2$, let $\rho_X$ be a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R^{d-1}$ with finite second moment, and define $s(t)=t|t|$ and $\sigma(t)=\max(t,0)$. For $\theta=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_d)\in\mathbb R^d$, define the signed-square ReLU feature in $L^2(\rho_X)$ by

$$\Phi(\theta)(x)=\sigma\!\left(\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}s(\theta_j)x_j+s(\theta_d)\right).$$

The two-copy parameterization uses this feature on one copy of $\mathbb R^d$ and its negative on the other copy; nonnegative measures on the disjoint union represent signed linear combinations of these features. The scalar signed-square map is continuously differentiable with derivative $s'(t)=2|t|$. This definition asserts differentiability of the resulting $L^2$ feature map only when its data law has the additional regularity needed for that conclusion; it does not assert that its differential is locally Lipschitz.

derivations.claim: On a small neighborhood of $(1,1)$ with $w,b>0$, the root $c(w,b)$ is a smooth function of parameters. For an increment $h=(h_1,h_2)$, $$r_{(w,b)+h}(x)-r_{w,b}(x)=2wh_1x+2bh_2+h_1^2x+h_2^2.$$ The candidate differential is $D\Phi_{(w,b)}h=\mathbf1_{x>c(w,b)}(2wh_1x+2bh_2)$. Outside the interval between $c(w,b)$ and $c((w,b)+h)$, the two preactivations have the same sign; there the ReLU remainder is either zero or $h_1^2x+h_2^2$, whose $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^2)$ by the finite second moment in [F1]. The interval between the two roots has length $O(|h|)$ and lies in a fixed bounded neighborhood of $-1$; on it the pointwise remainder is $O(|h|)$, so its $L^2(pdx)$ norm is $O(|h|^{3/2})$. Thus the full remainder is $o(|h|)$, proving Fréchet differentiability and the displayed differential.

At $(1,1)$ the derivative in direction $e_w=(1,0)$ is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-1}$. At $(1,1+\delta)$ it is $2x\mathbf1_{x>-(1+\delta)^2}$. For $0<\delta\le1/4$, their squared $L^2$ distance is $$4\int_{-(1+\delta)^2}^{-1}x^2p(x)\,dx\ge8p(2)\delta,$$ because the interval lies in $[-2,-1]$, where $x^2\ge1$ and $p(x)\ge p(2)$, and has length $2\delta+\delta^2\ge2\delta$. The operator norm difference of the two differentials is at least their difference on the unit vector $e_w$. Dividing by the parameter distance $\delta$ gives a quotient at least $\sqrt{8p(2)}/\sqrt\delta$, which diverges as $\delta\downarrow0$. Therefore the differential is not locally Lipschitz at $(1,1)$.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and Dependent Choice. For $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$, the following are equivalent:

1. $F$ is absolutely continuous.
2. $F'$ exists almost everywhere, $F'\in L^1[a,b]$, and
$$F(x)-F(a)=\int_a^xF'(t)\,dt\quad\text{for every }x\in[a,b].$$

Let $f:U\to V\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be totally differentiable at $a\in U$ and let $g:V\to\mathbb R^p$ be totally differentiable at $f(a)$. Then $g\circ f$ is totally differentiable at $a$ and

$$D(g\circ f)(a)=Dg(f(a))\circ Df(a).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

derivations.claim: We first prove a scalar gluing fact, without inferring absolute continuity of a composition with a merely continuous function. Let $I=[u,v]$, let $C\subseteq I$ be closed, let $h:I\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, and let $Q:I\to\mathbb R$ be absolutely continuous with $h=Q$ on $C$. Suppose that $Q'\le-\kappa$ a.e. on $C$, for some $\kappa>0$, and that $h(t)+\kappa t$ is nonincreasing on every component interval of $I\setminus C$, including its endpoints by continuity. Put $U=h+\kappa t$ and $Z=Q+\kappa t$. If $x<y$ both belong to $C$, the complementary open intervals $(\alpha_j,\beta_j)$ of $C$ inside $(x,y)$ have endpoints in $C$. Absolute continuity of $Z$ and countable additivity of its integrable derivative give $Z(y)-Z(x)=\int_{C\cap[x,y]}Z'(t)\,dt+\sum_j\int_{\alpha_j}^{\beta_j}Z'(t)\,dt$. The series is absolutely convergent because the intervals are disjoint and $Z'\in L^1$. Each gap integral equals $Z(\beta_j)-Z(\alpha_j)=U(\beta_j)-U(\alpha_j)\le0$, and the integral over $C$ is nonpositive. Thus $U(y)\le U(x)$. For arbitrary $x<y$, if $[x,y]$ misses $C$ they lie in one gap. Otherwise let $x_*=\min(C\cap[x,y])$ and $y_*=\max(C\cap[x,y])$; monotonicity on the two possible end gaps and the preceding inequality yield $U(y)\le U(y_*)\le U(x_*)\le U(x)$. Hence $h(y)-h(x)\le-\kappa(y-x)$ on all of $I$. This explicitly excludes positive singular variation on the closed contact set; no absolute continuity of $h$ has been assumed or concluded.

Let $d\ge1$, let $\mathcal H$ be a separable real Hilbert space, and let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^d$ be the closure of a nonempty convex open set. Let $R:\mathcal H\to[0,\infty)$ be differentiable, with differential Lipschitz on bounded sets in the uniform sense that for every bounded $B\subseteq\mathcal H$ there is a finite $L_B$ such that
$$\|dR_z-dR_{z'}\|_{\mathcal H^*}\le L_B\|z-z'\|_{\mathcal H}\qquad(z,z'\in B),$$
and bounded on every sublevel set of $R$. In particular, on each closed convex hull of a bounded feature image $\Phi(Q_r)$, both a finite Lipschitz constant $L_r$ and a finite norm bound $N_r$ for $dR$ are available. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to\mathcal H$ be Fréchet differentiable and let $V:\Omega\to[0,\infty)$ be $\lambda_V$-semiconvex, with the convention that $V(u)-\frac{\lambda_V}{2}|u|^2$ is convex on $\Omega$. For a semiconvex function $f$ on a convex domain $D$ with coefficient $\lambda$, define
$$\partial_\lambda f(u)=\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:f(v)\ge f(u)+\xi\cdot(v-u)+\tfrac{\lambda}{2}|v-u|^2\text{ for every }v\in D\}.$$
For a locally semiconvex function $g$ on $D$, define its local Fréchet subdifferential by
$$\partial g(u)=\left\{\xi\in\mathbb R^d:\liminf_{\substack{v\to u,\ v\in D\\v\ne u}}\frac{g(v)-g(u)-\xi\cdot(v-u)}{|v-u|}\ge0\right\}.$$
When $g$ is globally $\lambda$-semiconvex, this local subdifferential agrees with the convexified supporting set $\partial_\lambda g(u)$.
For every $r>0$, require a nonempty closed convex set $Q_r\subseteq\Omega$, nested increasingly in $r$, such that
$$\{u\in\Omega:\operatorname{dist}(u,Q_r)\le r'\}\subseteq Q_{r+r'}\qquad(r,r'>0),$$
such that $\Phi$ and $V$ are bounded on $Q_r$, $d\Phi$ is Lipschitz on $Q_r$, and there are fixed constants $C_1,C_2>0$ with
$$\sup_{u\in Q_r}\bigl(\|d\Phi_u\|+\|\partial V(u)\|\bigr)\le C_1+C_2r.$$
Here $\partial V(u)=\partial_{\lambda_V}V(u)$ is the supporting set on $\Omega$, and in the growth bound $\|\partial V(u)\|$ means its minimum element norm, equivalently the bound requires a supporting vector of norm at most $C_1+C_2r$ at every $u\in Q_r$. No bound is imposed on the domain normal cone. The source Assumptions 2.1 use the stronger maximal bound for the ambient potential subgradients before adding the domain indicator; that original bound implies the bounded-selection condition used here. Taking a supremum over the relative-domain supporting set would instead include unbounded normal vectors at proper-domain boundaries and would incorrectly exclude the constrained branch. All original source hypotheses and conclusions are retained by this sufficient, weaker growth convention. For a finite nonnegative Borel measure $\mu$ on $\mathbb R^d$, set
$$F(\mu)=R\!\left(\int_\Omega\Phi(u)\,d\mu(u)\right)+\int_\Omega V(u)\,d\mu(u)$$
when $\mu$ is concentrated on $\Omega$, the Bochner integral exists, and the scalar integral is finite; set $F(\mu)=+\infty$ otherwise. For $\mu\in\mathcal P_2(\Omega)$ with finite $F(\mu)$, write $m_\mu=\int_\Omega\Phi\,d\mu$ and define its first-variation potential on $\Omega$ by
$$F'(\mu)(u)=dR_{m_\mu}[\Phi(u)]+V(u).$$
No convexity of $R$ is required by this definition.

derivations.claim: Fix $s>0$ and two points $\theta_0,\theta_1\in\Theta$. Restrict the semiconvex inequality [F1] to the slice $w=s$ and divide it by $s$. Its quadratic error is bounded by $|\lambda|t(1-t)|\theta_1-\theta_0|^2/(2s)$. Letting $s\to\infty$ gives the convexity inequality for $W$, for every $0\le t\le1$.

If $\Theta=\mathbb R^q$, restrict $W$ to any line. A nonzero secant slope of a convex function forces its values to grow without bound in one of the two directions: for $a<b<c$, convexity makes the secant slope on $[b,c]$ at least that on $[a,b]$, and the reversed assertion treats a negative slope. Boundedness therefore makes every secant slope zero. Any two points lie on a line, so $W$ is constant.

In the bounded case $W$ attains its maximum at a point $x$ of the compact closure. At an interior maximum $dW_x=0$. At a boundary maximum its tangential differential is zero, because local $C^1$ boundary charts give two-sided differentiable curves in every tangent direction, while the Neumann hypothesis gives zero normal differential. These tangent and normal directions span the ambient space, so again $dW_x=0$. For any $y\in\Theta$, the one-variable convex function $t\mapsto W(x+t(y-x))$ has right derivative $dW_x(y-x)=0$; its secant slope is at least this derivative. Hence $W(y)\ge W(x)$, and maximality gives equality. The final reflected formulas follow by direct differentiation.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable space and let $\mu$ be a finite nonnegative measure on $(\mathbb R\times\Theta,\mathcal B(\mathbb R)\otimes\mathcal T)$ such that $\int|w|d\mu(w,\theta)<\infty$. Set $w_+=\max(w,0)$ and $w_-=\max(-w,0)$, and define finite nonnegative measures on $\Theta$ by

$$\alpha_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_+d\mu,\qquad\beta_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w_-d\mu\quad(B\in\mathcal T).$$

The partially one-homogeneous signed projection is

$$h^1(\mu)=\alpha_\mu-\beta_\mu,\qquad h^1(\mu)(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}w\,d\mu(w,\theta).$$

It is a finite signed measure. For every bounded measurable $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathbb R$, define its integral against this signed projection by

$\int_\Theta\varphi\,dh^1(\mu):=\int_\Theta\varphi d\alpha_\mu-\int_\Theta\varphi d\beta_\mu=\int_{\mathbb R\times\Theta}w\varphi(\theta)d\mu(w,\theta).$

Put $\lambda_\mu=\alpha_\mu+\beta_\mu$, so $\lambda_\mu(B)=\int_{\mathbb R\times B}|w|d\mu$. Its total variation satisfies $|h^1(\mu)|(B)\le\lambda_\mu(B)$ for every $B\in\mathcal T$. Therefore $\int\widetilde Vd|h^1(\mu)|\le\int |w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$ for every bounded nonnegative measurable $\widetilde V$.

If $\mathcal H$ is a separable real Hilbert space and $\varphi:\Theta\to\mathcal H$ is bounded and strongly measurable, then for every $z\in\mathcal H$ the feature moment satisfies $\langle z,\int w\varphi(\theta)d\mu\rangle=\int\langle z,\varphi(\theta)\rangle dh^1(\mu)$, with the scalar integral defined above. The raw measures $\alpha_\mu$ and $\beta_\mu$ record positive and negative parameter weights before cancellation and need not be mutually singular; for example, if $\mu$ assigns mass one to each of $(1,\theta_0)$ and $(-1,\theta_0)$ and zero elsewhere, then $\alpha_\mu=\beta_\mu$ both assign mass one to $\theta_0$ while $h^1(\mu)=0$. Thus the signed projection does not by itself determine a penalty of the form $\int|w|\widetilde V(\theta)d\mu$.

Assume DC. Let $X$ be a Banach space, $Y$ a normed space, and let $\mathcal F$ be a family of bounded linear operators $X\to Y$ ([[def-bounded-linear-operator]]). If $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|Tx\|<\infty$ for every $x\in X$, then $\sup_{T\in\mathcal F}\|T\|<\infty$, where the norm is [[def-operator-norm]].

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and $X$ a real or complex
Banach space. A strongly measurable function $f:\Omega\to X$ is
**Bochner integrable** if there is a sequence of integrable $X$-valued simple
functions $(s_n)$ such that

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega\|f-s_n\|\,d\mu=0.$$

For such a sequence define

$$\int_\Omega f\,d\mu:=\lim_{n\to\infty}\int_\Omega s_n\,d\mu.$$

The displayed norm limit exists: the simple integral inequality gives

$$\left\|\int s_n-\int s_m\right\|\leq\int\|s_n-s_m\|\leq\int\|s_n-f\|+\int\|f-s_m\|,$$

so the simple integrals form a Cauchy sequence, and $X$ is complete. The next
theorem proves that the value is independent of the approximating sequence and
characterizes existence by integrability of $\|f\|$.

For $E\in\mathcal A$, write
$\int_Ef\,d\mu:=\int_\Omega\mathbf1_Ef\,d\mu$ whenever this function is
Bochner integrable.

Let $f:\Omega\to X$ be strongly measurable. Then $f$ is Bochner integrable if
and only if

$$\int_\Omega\|f\|\,d\mu<\infty.$$

Here an a.e.-defined scalar function is integrated through any measurable
representative supplied by the strong simple approximation. Moreover the
Bochner integral is independent of the approximating sequence in its
definition.
